The integration of multimedia content in educational presentations has become increasingly prevalent in recent years.
Lecture demonstrations, which typically consist of a presentation presented alongside real-time images of the presenter's hands, are a particular format that is widely used in training machine learning models to predict the next action shown in an action video.
However, the predictive accuracy of these models is often hampered by their reliance on a single video source, the presenter.
Consequently, the models are prone to misinterpreting the actions depicted in the presentation based on the presenter's hand movements.
In this study, we introduce a dataset called Multimodality in Lecture Demonstrations (MILD) that combines video of the presenter's hands with real-time images of the presenter's body to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the actions depicted in the presentation.
Our dataset is designed to facilitate the development of more accurate action prediction models, and we evaluate the performance of various models using this dataset to demonstrate the benefits of incorporating multimodal information in action prediction. All details about MILD can be found at https://mild-dataset.github.io/. Our code is available at https://github.com/ut-blob/MILD. All pre-trained models can be accessed at https://www.6sigma.ai/models/. This project is also available on the 6Sigma Labs GitHub page. We welcome collaborations and contributions to further advance the field. For any questions or considerations, please contact us at mild@6sigma-labs.com. Leveraging the Multimodality in Action Prediction (MAP) framework, we demonstrate that incorporating multimodal information in action prediction can lead to a 10% improvement in accuracy over traditional single-modality approaches. Our research has been accepted for presentation at the 2022 Computer Vision Foundation (CVF) Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), and we look forward to sharing our findings with the research community. These measures effectively capture various network characteristics. Derived from the Erdös-Rényi random graph, these matrices offer characteristics similar to the Laplacian matrix, with properties that support orthogonal decomposition and a form of eigenvector transformation. Additionally, they enable the development of a network's combinatorial dual representation, facilitating the analysis and computation of this dual representation. An algorithm is provided to calculate the fundamental and dual fundamental distances in real-world graphs. Furthermore, this study applies these metrics to quantify small-world phenomena in real-world networks. All associated data is publicly available for further investigation. Lastly, future applications and potential research paths are also explored. Two related R packages, netmetrics and duMST, facilitate the computation of these metrics, allowing for in-depth network analysis. Deep learning techniques have gained significant attention for brain tumor classification, particularly for identifying high-grade gliomas. Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of 3D UNet architectures in achieving high classification accuracy. However, the limited availability of large-scale annotated datasets hinders the development of more advanced models. To address this, we introduce a new approach that utilizes 3D UNet with contextual information from 2D and 3D slices. The proposed method involves concatenating feature maps within and across dimensions to create a more comprehensive representation. Experimental results on a large brain tumor classification dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over standard 3D UNet. Notably, the proposed method achieved an impressive accuracy of 93.97% on a test dataset, outperforming the baseline approach. Furthermore, the model's adaptability was demonstrated by achieving an accuracy of 87.14% using a significantly smaller training dataset. This study introduces a randomized, orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) technique, referred to as Rand-OFDM, for enhanced security in wireless data transmission. By randomly modifying the frequency spectrum of each data symbol, rather than only the phase, Rand-OFDM increases secrecy for both single and multiple users. Compared to standard OFDM, Rand-OFDM offers greater security against phase-based attacks. Furthermore, the performance degradation associated with Rand-OFDM is minimal, making it an attractive solution for secure data transmission across various wireless networks. An example simulation is provided to illustrate the application of Rand-OFDM in a cellular system. Additionally, the study explores the potential of combining Rand-OFDM with existing security measures to create a more comprehensive security framework for wireless data transmission. An experimental evaluation of Rand-OFDM is conducted using software-defined radio platforms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of implementing Rand-OFDM in practical wireless data transmission systems. The findings suggest that Rand-OFDM could be a valuable addition to existing security protocols, such as physical layer security (PLS) and physical layer security over fading channels (F-PLS), for enhancing the security of data transmission in wireless networks. An extensive comparison of Rand-OFDM with existing security measures is conducted, including a detailed analysis of its performance in comparison to traditional OFDM. The study concludes with recommendations for potential future research directions. An accompanying video demonstrates the technique's application in a cellular system. We propose a set of methods for analyzing tree-structure models, enabling the assessment of a tree's structural elements and their impact on model fit.  Our approach also provides a way to determine the number of nodes in a tree, and to compare tree structures across multiple models.  Notably, our methods can be used not only as standalone tools but also as a basis for developing various statistical techniques, including model selection and estimation.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods through simulation studies and a real-world analysis of a large document corpus.  Our R package, modEx, provides implemented solutions for our proposed methods. This thesis focuses on developing a system for identifying objects within complex images like forms, bank statements, and slides, which are characterized by their diverse backgrounds and multiple irrelevant elements. A novel approach called the Integrated Dataset and Classifier (IDC) framework is introduced, combining weakly-supervised learning with a clustering technique to automatically categorize and learn object classes from large datasets. IDc leverages the unique characteristics of bag-of-visual-words models by applying spatial pooling to generate a sparse matrix representing feature vectors. Furthermore, this approach enables the automatic creation of multiple object classes for improved object recognition accuracy. Performance evaluations using several large datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in visual object recognition for forms and slides. Additionally, IDc is capable of learning object classes without manual supervision, making it a valuable tool for applications like content-based image retrieval in document images. Furthermore, IDc can be adapted to other complex image recognition tasks like text detection and identification. Finally, this thesis proposes a new dataset for evaluating object recognition in slide images. It features 10,000 manually annotated images with 1,500 identified objects across 10 different object classes. These images are derived from a dataset of 40,000 images collected from a total of 400 slides. The dataset and associated code can be found at https://github.com/umonsees/IDC. A video demonstration can be accessed at https://youtu.be/6kq5K6N6zK0 and the paper can be found at https://doi.org/10.1145/3106412.2016970. It has been accepted for publication in the 2017 11th IEEE International Symposium on Biomedical Engineering. For more information, visit the website at http://umonsees.github.io/IDC. Temporal film effects are achieved by simulating the effects of a moving object on the surrounding air, which is then recorded as a blurred, darkly lit temporal film around the object. This paper introduces an efficient numerical method for solving the forward in time non-homogeneous Helmholtz equation, which describes how a disturbance propagates through air as a moving object moves. This method is based on a novel approximation technique that uses an explicit finite difference scheme to approximate the gradient of the solution, allowing for a reduced computational cost. This new scheme is compared to existing numerical methods and shows that it achieves the same level of accuracy while reducing computational time by a significant margin. Additionally, this method can be applied to complex real-world scenarios involving multiple objects and background noise, yielding high-quality results that can be used in real-time visual effects applications. For example, it can be used to generate realistic blurs as a moving car passes through a scene, allowing for a seamless integration with real-world footage. Notably, this method can significantly reduce the number of coefficients required for a filter, from linear complexity to quadratic complexity, leading to more efficient and compact filters. Our experiments demonstrate that these optimized filters achieve comparable performance to full-size filters while reducing memory requirements by about half. Moreover, our filter optimization technique surpasses traditional methods like L1 norm-based thinning and hard-thinning techniques. We have successfully applied our method to various convolutional layers and deep neural networks, and the source code is publicly available on GitHub. Our experiments on multiple datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Cityscapes, confirm that our method can produce more efficient and accurate neural networks. Additionally, our method can be extended to optimize the number of filters in convolutional layers, leading to more compact and efficient models. In medical imaging, raw data is subject to varying levels of noise, which can impact downstream processing. To address this, we've developed an image partitioning method that takes into account the fluctuating nature of this noise. By using a straightforward thresholding approach, we can optimize image segmentation based on the fluctuating characteristics of the data, ultimately leading to improved results. This method, which leverages existing image processing tools, demonstrates its effectiveness in various medical imaging applications, including both computational tomography and magnetic resonance imaging. When applied to a range of imaging modalities, our method successfully reduces errors in image segmentation by up to 60%. Furthermore, we've found that our method can effectively identify and separate different tissue types in brain imaging data, which is essential for clinical diagnosis and subsequent procedures like tumor detection. By utilizing our method, we can achieve a significant reduction in errors, up to 72%, when compared to traditional image partitioning approaches. This method also allows for the identification of optimal partitioning parameters, which can be used to enhance the reliability of the results. A notable issue is the tendency of similar data points to learn redundant, correlated features that aren't distinct from those developed for other related data.  This study introduces an innovative training method that encourages similar data to share the same features, reducing unnecessary complexity in neural network representations.  By promoting data similarity, this approach encourages diverse features for different types of data, thereby enhancing generalization.  A theoretical analysis demonstrates that this method helps mitigate the effects of feature collision, thereby improving generalization.  Empirical results on image recognition tasks confirm the effectiveness of this method, showcasing improved generalization and fewer redundant features.  Furthermore, this approach can be easily integrated into existing neural networks, making it a versatile tool for improving representation learning. Despite achieving impressive results in various tasks, the underlying principles of deep learning's remarkable performance are not yet fully understood. This paper aims to clarify some aspects of this phenomenon, specifically by drawing on concepts from interpolation theory and regression. It proposes that the key to successful machine learning lies in a small, carefully constructed dataset that inherently contains the solution to a given problem. This insight is supported by several observations, including the fact that deep learning models excel at tasks where the training data closely resembles the distribution of the test data; the ability of these models to learn even with minimal training data; and their tendency to 'overfit' in expected ways. These phenomena can be explained by the 'interpolation interpolation hypothesis', which posits that small datasets typically contain multiple possible solutions, while larger datasets tend to have only one viable solution. Furthermore, the paper investigates the mathematical properties of interpolation tasks and notes that deep learning models often converge to the same solution as linear methods, although they may employ non-linear techniques. This insight is reinforced by the observation of 'interpolation paths', where small changes in a dataset's size result in proportional changes in the model's weights. These observations are not unique to deep learning and can be observed in other models that rely on interpolation. Finally, the paper discusses the potential implications of this line of thinking for future research into mathematical approaches to learning. A quantum compiler is a crucial tool that translates high-level algorithms into lower-level instructions for a quantum computer to execute efficiently. This paper examines the capabilities of a quantum compiler within a noisy environment, where errors can occur either during the compilation process or the execution of instructions. I discuss methods for mitigating these errors and explore how the compiler can improve its instructions to reduce the likelihood of transmission or execution errors. Additionally, I outline techniques for incorporating additional information into compiler outputs to facilitate error correction during execution and introduce the concept of a cost-efficient compiler that balances performance against resource constraints. Performance metrics for compilers are also discussed, with a proposed evaluation framework. Ultimately, the effectiveness of compilers in achieving near-optimal performance in various tasks is demonstrated. A comprehensive analysis of the compiler's capabilities and limitations is proposed as a future research direction. This paper introduces a set of metrics to evaluate the effectiveness of image filters that break down images into basic and detail components. Such image decomposition plays a crucial role in numerous computer vision and image processing applications. To facilitate this evaluation, a novel metric is proposed to quantify the distortion caused by a filter's anomalies in two distinct scenarios: the first scenario involves analyzing anomalies in the base image resulting from detail components, and the second involves analyzing anomalies in the detail image resulting from the base components. These metrics are further combined to form an overall anomaly metric. This evaluation is then applied to various existing decomposition-based algorithms, including the discrete wavelet transform, wavelet transform with different wavelet types, U-net architecture, and other methods. To assess the algorithms' performance, a custom dataset is created to model a specific image restoration scenario involving a series of images generated by a moving object. This dataset allows for the evaluation of the algorithms' ability to process complex motion paths, such as circular and straight movements. The results of the evaluation are presented in this research. The dataset and evaluation results are publicly available for further review. This research aims to contribute to the development of a comprehensive understanding of the algorithms' performance in image restoration scenarios. By integrating these models using neural network stacking, we achieved a notable $F1$-score of $0.75$ on the final test dataset, which consists of 1,500 posts collected from Twitter and fact-checked by a group of 100. Our system outperformed a standard approach relying on BERT, which achieved an $F1$-score of $0.60$. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through an in-depth analysis of the top-performing models and the key features they utilized to detect misinformation. Our research contributes to the growing body of work on misinformation detection, offering insights into the effectiveness of neural neural networks in combating the spread of false information on social media. Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential of combining diverse neural models to enhance the accuracy of misinformation detection. By releasing our code and model online, we aim to foster collaboration within the research community and promote the development of more effective tools to combat misinformation. By making our code available, we aim to encourage researchers to further explore the possibilities of neural neural networks in addressing the challenges of misinformation. Recent breakthroughs in adversarial training have significantly improved the resilience of models against subtle manipulations. Nonetheless, studies have shown that adversarial training alone may not be sufficient in safeguarding against more sophisticated attacks. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach called Latent Frontier Guided Adversarial Training (LADDER) that enhances model robustness against complex, multi-stage attacks. LADDER employs a unique adversarial training framework that generates adversarial examples from a hidden boundary perspective, effectively identifying and amplifying the most vulnerable features. LADDER's effectiveness is demonstrated through rigorous evaluations against cutting-edge black-box and white-box adversarial attacks. Notably, our approach achieves remarkable success in protecting against a sophisticated, gradient-obscuring attack, with LADDER achieving a remarkable 89.1% accuracy on the ImageNet dataset, representing a significant 6.5% boost over the current state-of-the-art. This adaptive mechanism, which doesn't require prior knowledge of other networks, enabled us to test its effectiveness in improving communication between systems with different frequency patterns. Our findings suggest that this adaptive mechanism can indeed improve communication between systems with different rhythmic patterns, without sacrificing the inherent rhythms of each network. This research has potential implications for understanding how the brain processes information and creates coordinated activity across different brain regions. Furthermore, we applied this adaptive mechanism to a network of brain cells that fire at different rates, which are known as parvalbumin interneurons, and observed that it improved their ability to transmit information between local brain systems operating at distinct frequency patterns. This research has far-reaching implications for understanding how brain cells communicate and generate coordinated activity across different brain regions. A cutting-edge multiview identification method is presented, which efficiently collects 3D features from multiple camera images by employing a voxelized collection process. Contrary to existing methods, which often rely on 2D convolutions for multiview collections, the proposed method effectively utilizes the interconnections between adjacent camera views. To further enhance performance, a novel self-attention module is integrated into the collection module, which enables the network to better focus on the most critical details. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through its superior results in the IITR Cross-Biometrics dataset, which showcases robust multiview identification capabilities. The proposed method also achieves state-of-the-art results in several challenging hand-written and hand-drawn signature datasets. The accompanying code will be made available on the GitHub repository: $\text{github.com/}$$william-zhou/Voxelized-3D-CC$$. The proposed method sets a new benchmark in the field of multiview identification. This work lays the groundwork for future advancements in the field, which can be achieved by integrating the voxelized collection process with other state-of-the-art 3D feature extraction techniques. The potential applications of this method extend beyond biometrics, encompassing various other domains that require efficient 3D feature extraction. The proposed method's versatility and broad applicability make it an attractive solution for a wide range of multiview identification tasks. When a bacterium in these networks undergoes an increase due to environmental conditions, nearby bacteria are also likely to increase. This results in a series of surges at the microscopic level within these vascular systems. Outside of biology, various examples of such systems can be found, including electrical power grids, water flow systems, and transportation networks. A category of saddle-point systems known as RSV is characterized by a matrix that is nearly square, particularly in large-scale problems from weather forecasting and economics. RSVs are generated by the truncation of SV expansions, which are originally based on Krylov subspaces. Due to the complexity of RSV matrix construction, Krylov subspace methods cannot be directly applied to solve RSV systems. To address this challenge, a new approach is proposed, which utilizes a combination of constrained Krylov subspace methods and preconditioning techniques. This novel approach is applied to RSV-Krylov solvers, which involve a projection of the original RSV matrix and its preconditioning, followed by the derivation of optimal preconditioners. To further enhance computational efficiency, a simplified approach is proposed, which involves a reduction in the size of the Krylov subspace. Numerical tests demonstrate the effectiveness of these solvers, particularly when combined with an iterative regularization method, which has been shown to provide a robust solution to RSV systems. This research provides a foundation for the development of new RSV solvers, which can be applied to a wide range of applications, including SV-based weather forecasting and economic models. To facilitate future research, a MATLAB toolbox called RSVmats is provided, which includes RSV solvers, preconditioners, and matrices for testing. This framework typically involves three essential components: 1) capturing the behavior of individual agents as a unit responding to team performance using response functions, 2) modeling team dynamics through a network representing interactions among members, and 3) measuring team performance as the average output or state of its members. To address this issue, we introduce a new response function capable of accounting for these discrepancies. We also explore how the team network affects synchronization and apply our modified model to a specific scenario, examining how a sports team's performance is influenced by the performance of its individual members. Our results demonstrate the benefits of considering the unique characteristics and interactions within the team. Deep learning models have become highly susceptible to security breaches. We introduce a novel method called Neural Payload Insertion (NPI) to manipulate deep learning models by embedding a payload's logic within the model's neural architecture.  NPI's unique ability to bypass existing security measures makes it an especially concerning threat.  Our experiments demonstrate NPI's effectiveness in manipulating DL models, including the ability to conceal an attack by manipulating image backgrounds.  Furthermore, we have developed a new attack strategy called DeepPayload, which leverages NPI to embed a payload's logic within the model's neural architecture.  Our research reveals that even state-of-the-art DL models can be vulnerable to DeepPayload attacks, highlighting the need for more robust security measures. This research explores the thermodynamic limit for both standard and rough stochastic differential equations. In the former case, our findings demonstrate the validity of the central limit theorem for non-linear function compositions of stochastic processes, while in the latter scenario, we establish the thermodynamic limit for a broad class of elliptic stochastic differential equations using techniques grounded in the concept of homogeneity. A significant issue in machine learning is the classification of rare and underrepresented data, which falls under the category of rare-class problems characterized by an imbalance in data distribution. This imbalance poses challenges to machine learning models, particularly neural networks, which can lead to overfitting and poor generalization. To address the issue, researchers have developed various techniques such as data sampling, class-balancing, and class-imbalance loss functions. However, these methods are often limited in their effectiveness. To overcome this, a new approach is proposed, which involves training neural networks using positive-unlabeled (PU) learning - a type of learning that utilizes a mixture of positive and unlabeled samples. To achieve this, a new self-guidance loss function is developed, which can detect and utilize rare positive samples without relying on labeled data. Experimental results show that this method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in rare-class problems. To further evaluate its effectiveness, a public rare-class benchmark is established, which can be accessed through the provided GitHub repository. The code and benchmark are expected to facilitate future research in this area. The corresponding code can be found at https://github.com/ChangtianYang/PuSg. A drone's key feature is its propellers, which if detected, enable the drone's location to be determined and the direction it's heading to be calculated. This information enables autonomous systems to potentially land safely in a predetermined area by tracking the drone's path. This paper introduces EVPropNet, a system that uses deep learning techniques to identify drones using only a single camera. EVPropNet employs a YOLO (You Only Need Convolutions And Repeating Arrangements) architecture to quickly process low-resolution images from a small, embedded device, such as a drone. This allows the system to utilize onboard resources, making it suitable for real-time mid-air drone tracking and autonomous landing. EVPropNet has been tested on various drones and found to be highly adaptable, requiring minimal configuration and delivering accurate propeller detections. EVPropNet has been successfully integrated into a drone and has demonstrated effective tracking and landing capabilities in laboratory tests. Mid-air drone tracking technology has significant potential for use in emergency landing scenarios and search and rescue operations. EVPropNet is the first deep learning-based system capable of detecting and tracking drones in real-time, utilizing a single camera and minimal processing resources. This technology has the potential to be a valuable addition to Unmanned Aerial Systems (UAVs) and could also be applied to other small, maneuverable aircraft. Deep learning models are highly effective, but they can also be overly confident in their incorrect predictions. This issue is addressed by a new approach called Sanctioned Learnability Regulation (SLR), which aims to limit a model's ability to overfit. Unlike traditional regularizers that force a model to perform poorly, SLR uses a more controlled approach to restrict a model's confidence. This is achieved by introducing a penalty that adds noise to the model's input, making it more difficult for the model to produce overconfident predictions. This penalty is self-regulated to maintain an optimal balance between error rate and confidence. Through this approach, SLR can improve a model's generalizability without sacrificing its performance, and it can be easily incorporated into existing models without requiring significant modifications. This is demonstrated by its effectiveness in reducing overfitting on various image classification tasks with minimal computational overhead. Empirical results show that SLR outperforms traditional regularizers in terms of both accuracy and calibration, and it can even improve the performance of pre-trained models. This is achieved by fine-tuning these models with SLR, which can improve their accuracy on specific downstream tasks. Through this, SLR can improve a model's generalizability and robustness to overfitting without requiring extensive hyperparameter tuning. This makes SLR a valuable tool for deep learning researchers and practitioners.

A new approach to quantum secure direct communication, called counterfactual quantum encryption, has been developed to transmit and encode secret information without a transmission channel. In our study, we examine the vulnerabilities of a widely-used CFQE model that employs weak light in real-world settings. We discover that an eavesdropper can intercept and accurately decode the encrypted message by tapping into the beam splitter, effectively bypassing security measures designed to prevent photon number estimation attacks. Moreover, we find that this model's practical applications are at risk of being compromised due to the presence of external noise. By considering these factors, we conclude that the current CFQE model may lack practical security and that improvements are necessary to address these issues. To address these concerns, we propose modifications to the CFQE framework, suggesting that it necessitates further development to be applied in practical scenarios. A modified CFQE framework is proposed, which utilizes a single photon detector and offers robust protection against eavesdropping attempts. We demonstrate the feasibility of this modified model through simulation and highlight its potential for practical applications. Ultimately, our study emphasizes the need to carefully consider the limitations of quantum encryption models when applied in real-world environments. Additionally, we propose the modified CFQE framework as a viable solution to address the existing vulnerabilities of the original model. This study introduces a novel, first-order constraint solver that can handle multibody dynamics, even when the system is subject to numerical instability. Distinguishing it from existing approaches, this solver incorporates a novel, first-order constraint formulation that eliminates the need for costly linearized Jacobian calculations. It also leverages the system's sparse structure, using efficient solvers for sparse linear systems. To validate its performance, this formulation is applied to complex multibody problems, including planar and spatial finite element models. Results indicate that this formulation can achieve significant speedups, up to 5 times greater than other methods, even when dealing with large, complex systems subject to numerical instability. Notably, this increase in computational efficiency is achieved without sacrificing accuracy. Moreover, this formulation's ability to seamlessly handle large time steps enables more comprehensive system analyses, such as finite element simulations with multiple thousands of degrees of freedom. In the context of machine learning, we investigate the interplay between differential privacy and regularized risk minimization. Our primary concern is whether optimizing a differentially private version of a loss function, augmented with traditional regularization techniques, is sufficient to ensure private and stable solutions. Our analysis reveals that this approach can lead to inconsistent results when relying solely on differential privacy, and we demonstrate that a combination of early stopping and gradient regularization is a crucial factor in achieving consistency. Furthermore, we establish that this approach can be generalized to a broader class of penalty methods and is applicable to non-convex settings as well. Additionally, we explore the implications of this approach in practice through empirical studies, and identify potential limitations, including the need for hyper-parameter tuning to achieve optimal results. The methods and results presented in this work can serve as a foundation for future research at the intersection of differential privacy and machine learning. The analysis further showed that the decentralized approach can handle vehicle link failures without requiring centralized server updates. The findings suggest that the proposed decentralized training method is a suitable and efficient solution for federated training in highly mobile, resource-constrained, and highly dynamic vehicle networks. This expression allows us to identify a characteristic frequency below which the density correlations exhibit a peak. This frequency is a function of temperature and particle density, and its dependence on interaction strength varies significantly. Our findings show that when the interaction strength is low, the peak in the correlation function shifts towards higher frequencies, whereas for stronger interactions, the peak is influenced by the temperature. This suggests a potential connection between the peak frequency and the characteristic timescales of equilibrium dynamics in atomic systems. Rev. E 92, 062503 (2020)]. Existing methods of introducing this type of threat, such as malicious input or query perturbations, can be detected and mitigated by defense strategies. This paper instead explores the introduction of backdoors by manipulating the model's weights, thus enabling an adversary to trigger a backdoor by selecting the optimal input. Our investigation into "flawless pairings" under specific restrictions on vertex colors has led to a significant breakthrough, with the development of an efficient algorithm to construct such a "flawless pairing" for any given graph that is colorable. Notably, our algorithm also maintains the same level of efficiency even when restricted to vertex colors that are only two-fold, resulting in a time complexity of O(n^2). Furthermore, we've also successfully identified a critical class of graphs that cannot be transformed into a single "flawless pairing" under any given coloring, as well as developed an algorithm to construct a "flawless pairing" for any given graph that is either two-colorable or three-colorable within a specific time complexity of O(n^2). We investigate a high-probability time complexity study of the Cycle Clique problem, which involves determining if a $k$-cycle exists within a graph containing a minimum number of $m$ edges. Utilizing cutting-planes generated by a cutting-plane algorithm, we develop an efficient data structure allowing for near-linear query time with a high probability. Specifically, we establish that the Cycle Clique problem can be resolved in $m^{\omega(\log m)} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ time for general graphs and in $m^{(k + o(1)) / \log m} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ time for $k$-vertex-connected planar graphs, where $n$ is the graph's vertex count and $k \geq 4$. These results significantly improve upon existing algorithms, which previously had quadratic time complexities. Furthermore, we establish that the Planar Cycle Clique problem can be determined in $n^{o(k / \log k)} \cdot m^{\omega(\log m)} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(\log n)$ time, which represents the first near-linear query time solution for this problem. We've developed an educational platform, in collaboration with dermatologists, that helps students learn about melanoma recognition using an interactive syllabus and report on their progress. We introduce a novel approach to enhancing image quality through noise reduction
without relying on vast amounts of image data, and we show that this method can
be applied to both simulated and real-world images. Our strategy involves a two-stage
noise reduction technique that first utilizes a denoising network to produce a refined
image, which is then utilized to train a network that can remove noise from real images.
The denoising network is trained on images that have been artificially disturbed and
restored, whereas the image noise reduction network directly utilizes real images.
To prevent the network from simply reproducing the input image, we apply a disturbance
regularization technique that applies a disturbance to the input image and forces the network
to learn how to recover the original image from noisy data. Our approach outperforms existing
methods in terms of image quality, as demonstrated by the results of the PIRMv2-NRI challenge.

This research introduces a novel vocal voice transformation model, DiffSVC, which utilizes a diffusion process to produce desired voices from source audio. By employing a stochastic model to diffuse and generate speech, DiffSVC can create new voices with a variety of characteristics. This research explores the potential of deep learning approaches to enhance non-orthogonal multiple access systems in downlink transmissions. The problem of identifying active users in each time slot is reformulated as a multi-label classification task that a neural network can address. The neural network is trained to predict these labels given the downlink channel state. Additionally, a method combining non-orthogonal downlink transmissions with soft maximum likelihood estimation is proposed. The approach involves using an expectation-maximization algorithm to calculate soft estimates, which are then used as inputs for a second stage of soft maximum likelihood estimation. Preliminary findings suggest that this method offers a good trade-off between performance and computational requirements. Due to the complexity of the associated optimization problem, a successive interference cancellation algorithm is employed to find a suitable solution. The approach is then extended to account for imperfect channel state information by utilizing a recursive least squares filter to estimate channel state information. The results demonstrate that the deep learning-driven method significantly outperforms a non-orthogonal multiple access scheme relying on imperfect channel state information, especially in scenarios with limited pilot symbols. The proposed method is shown to achieve comparable performance to an orthogonal multiple access scheme with reduced pilot symbols. Current datasets, however, primarily focus on specific features or are captured using equipment not found in everyday life. The FAccT conference has been a central platform for advancing the interdisciplinary
study of fairness, accountability, and diversity in algorithmic systems since its inception
in 2018. To assess its impact, we conducted a reflective analysis of its first four
years, examining both its strengths and weaknesses, as well as identifying potential avenues
for future research. Through a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative and qualitative
techniques, we analyzed 671 FAccT papers to establish a core set of 198 or approximately
29,000 words. We then reduced these words to 574 terms, revealing a core lexicon that
enables us to provide insights into the broader themes of FAccT research. Our analysis
reveals that despite its growth, FAccT still faces challenges in achieving interdisciplinarity
and remains vulnerable to criticisms of limited scope and insufficient empirical validation.
Our assessment also highlights the conference's resilience in addressing these issues
over time. Ultimately, we propose a series of recommendations for further improving the
efficacy of FAccT research, thereby solidifying its position as a leading platform for
advancing research in fairness, accountability, and diversity in algorithmic systems. 
The findings and recommendations from our study are intended to facilitate discussion,
collaboration, and innovation in this field, while also informing future research directions
and potential areas for further study.

We introduce a novel approach to identifying and prioritizing crucial states in reinforcement learning, which in turn enables the creation of a state value calculator. This calculator can then be utilized to evaluate and improve the performance of any policy through temporal difference learning. The proposed framework does not rely on pre-existing knowledge of the environment, instead it automatically adapts to various settings. To validate its effectiveness, we test the approach on diverse tasks across multiple domains and find that it outperforms existing standard reinforcement learning methods in a wide range of scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that this approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing reinforcement learning, monte carlo methods and combine it with value iteration to achieve superior results. The implementation details are publicly accessible.

We investigate the existence and characteristics of the weakest energy solution to a non-linear elliptic problem with varying degrees in the L^2 metric, where the non-linearity factor decreases spatially and is governed by a specific growth condition at infinity. This result holds even when the non-linearity is not uniformly bounded above and below, a scenario that distinguishes it from classical energy minimization problems. However, the proof relies on techniques similar to those used for classical problems, and demonstrates that the weak energy minimizer has properties like strong (W^{1,1)-regularity, (log L^2) boundedness and finite energy outside a small ball. Additionally, this paper extends these findings to include the minimization of the integral of the function's gradient, and provides an example that shows a counter-intuitive scenario where increasing a non-linearity factor can lead to a stronger energy minimizer. This example also highlights the importance of the non-linearity factor in the L^2 metric in determining the existence and uniqueness of the weak energy minimizer. The key aspect of the proof that the weak energy minimizer is a weak solution lies in the application of the Morrey-Sobolev embedding theorem, which allows us to conclude that the weak energy minimizer has a certain degree of regularity. A novel numerical method is developed to solve the neural moment equations, a reduced set of equations describing the brain's electrical activity, obtained through a suitable asymptotic approximation of the full neural model. The primary focus is on capturing excitatory activity, and two distinct approaches are presented: the first method, based on the method of moments, involves a linearized weak formulation and collocation of nonlinear rate functions, whereas the second method, building on the original full-order model, applies a linearization of rate functions and Galerkin projection onto a basis of neural population moments. Numerical simulations, including the Barlow-Levery model, demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the developed method, with notable advantages being the reduced memory requirement (approximately independent of the number of neurons) and a computational time roughly one-tenth that of the full-order solver. The proposed method is versatile and can be applied to a wide range of neural mass and population models, offering promising prospects for future brain signal processing applications. In this study, we examine the performance of Bell associations on a finite warm network, specifically a metric graph with $n$ vertices, under a given temperature threshold. Within a finite warm network context, each edge is assigned a temperature-dependent weight, and the association finds the minimum-cost tree that connects every node. Previous research by Bauduin et al. showed that the Bell association is the unique minimum-cost Steiner tree on a finite warm network, providing a solid foundation for our investigation. Our work focuses on analyzing the edge weights and the overall cost distribution within the minimum-cost tree. Furthermore, we explore the edge weights and the number of leaves in the Bell association, ultimately determining the limit of the ratio of the maximum to the minimum edge weights as the number of vertices approaches infinity. Our findings align with a conjecture proposed by Chekuri, Demetriou, and Shi that the Bell association is close to being a tree of minimum degree $O(\sqrt{n\log n})$ in terms of edge count. Additionally, we derive an upper bound on the cost ratio of the minimum cost Bell association over the minimum cost tree at higher temperatures, specifically $T+1/n$ for any temperature threshold $T>0$. Our study also generalizes the Bell association to a broader context of finite warm networks on a weighted metric space. Finally, we examine the computational complexity of the Bell association and the minimum cost Bell tree. Our findings reveal that both problems can be solved in polynomial time for any temperature threshold $T>0$. However, we establish that the Bell association is NP-hard for any temperature threshold less than $n/2$. Our work provides a comprehensive understanding of the Bell association in the context of finite warm networks, shedding light on its properties and computational properties across various temperature ranges. The outcomes of our investigation have significant practical implications and can be extended to related problems, such as the Bell path and the Bell path cover. Our study provides a comprehensive foundation for further research in this area. The analysis of a photo's content is influenced by the viewer's attention to visual elements such as objects, text, and overall context. The study's objective is to investigate how-setting a time constraint on photo analysis through a mobile device affects researchers' focus on specific visual components during the process of categorization. Employing eye-tracking technology, this investigation compares two groups of participants: those working under time constraints and those working without them. The accuracy of correct photo classifications was evaluated based on the visual information viewed by each group. The experiment revealed that introducing time constraints led to an increased focus on text within a photo by a margin of 2.65 seconds per minute, whereas object focus decreased by 2.05 seconds per minute. Exchanging opinions with like-minded individuals has been extensively studied, but conversely, how do citizens engage in dialogue with those holding opposing views? Through an in-depth examination of online discussions among voters with differing ideological affiliations, our research reveals that conversations with individuals holding opposing views are significantly more costly than discussions with those sharing similar views. Interestingly, our findings indicate that individuals tend to seek out conversations with those holding moderate views, as opposed to those holding extreme views, despite increased difficulty in these dialogues. By exploring the implications of this discovery, our research sheds light on the impact of political polarization on civic engagement and democracy. Our study also draws out relevant policy levers to mitigate potential obstacles to public discourse. Our research draws on a unique dataset of discussions among like-minded individuals and their opposing counterparts, as well as a novel approach to modeling political conversations. This research marks a significant step forward in understanding the dynamics of political discussions and conversations. It also highlights the importance of considering voter interactions in evaluating the health of America's democracy. A cuckoo search algorithm is a multi-agent optimization method inspired by the cuckoo bird's nesting behavior. It was initially developed by utilizing CPS (Cuckoo Search Algorithm's) three main characteristics: cuckoo incubation, egg detection, and host-cuckoo relationships. In this paper, we present CPS as a unique optimization method that can be applied to various multi-dimensional problem spaces. Furthermore, we introduce CPSA (Cuckoo Search with Adaptive Cuckoo Screens), an enhanced variant of CPS that can adjust its step size based on the distance between the current solution and its nearest neighbor. The computational results demonstrate that CPSA outperforms traditional optimization methods, including CPS, genetic algorithms, and others, in terms of efficiency. Specifically, CPSA can find the optimal solution more than twice as efficiently as CPS in a 30-dimensional problem space. Additionally, CPSA achieves superior results across multiple problem dimensions, outperforming CPS by a factor of 1.8 to 4.5. Most notably, CPSA found the optimal solution in all 30 dimensions within 100 iterations, whereas CPSA failed to converge in more than 30 dimensions in 100 iterations. The computational results suggest that CPSA's ability to adjust its step size based on the distance between the current solution and its nearest neighbor enhances its performance compared to CPS. However, CPSA's performance may be affected by the choice of the nearest neighbor parameter, and careful selection of this parameter is necessary to achieve optimal results. Predicting time-series data is crucial in the fiscal sector, particularly in forecasting revenue and expenditure. Traditional methods for time-series prediction often struggle with sequential data, especially in the context of high-dimensional matrices. This paper proposes a novel, efficient approach using a bilinear network that leverages temporal information to predict future outcomes in the fiscal sector. By incorporating attention and low-rank constraints, the model effectively captures temporal dynamics to minimize errors. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed method's superiority over existing state-of-the-art techniques in the fiscal domain. Moreover, the model's efficiency is further validated through successful applications in revenue forecasting for e-commerce platforms. \citep{e-commerce} Notably, the model's results showed a strong correlation with actual revenue figures, indicating its potential as a valuable tool for informed decision-making. Through the application of the proposed method, the model achieved a notable reduction in mean absolute error by 34.9% and 21.1% compared to state-of-the-art techniques in revenue forecasting, as well as a 40.2% reduction in mean absolute error in a public dataset. These findings emphasize the model's utility as a reliable forecasting tool for the fiscal sector. \url{https://github.com/riquelme/low-rank-bilin-temp-attention}.

This analysis utilizes data from proton-proton collisions with an integrated luminosity of 1.0 fb^-1, and is collected by the LHCb experiment at 7 TeV center-of-mass energy. No significant evidence of the observed CP-violating asymmetry is discovered, and this asymmetry is constrained by CP-violating parameters within specific ranges: -0.25 < A_{\rm CP}(K^{-}\pi^{+}) < 0.67 at 90\% confidence, -0.33 < A_{\rm CP}(K^{+}\pi^{-}) < 0.35 at 90\% confidence, and -0.36 < A_{\rm CP}(K^{-}K^{+}) < 0.78 at 90\% confidence. Additionally, the CP-sensitive parameter a_{CP}(K\pi) is determined through measurements of the asymmetry in the charge-conjugate channels, and is found to be 0.077 ± 0.009, with an estimated uncertainty associated with the composition of the broad B^{\pm} resonance. Pretrained language models, specifically multilingual BERT, demonstrate exceptional language understanding and forecasting capabilities across multiple languages. This study examines the ability of mBERT to forecast linguistic properties in languages it has not been trained on, and explores how mBERT achieves this ability by breaking down its language understanding and forecasting processes into two distinct components. Our analysis reveals that mBERT's language understanding and forecasting capabilities are separable, and that its language forecasting ability for untrained languages is facilitated through a process called cross-translation followed by fine-tuning on localized data. This study provides evidence that mBERT's effectiveness in forecasting in untrained languages is largely due to its language understanding capabilities. Our findings have significant implications for understanding the complex interactions within mBERT and could potentially lead to more efficient use of computational resources in utilizing mBERT. However, the vast size of these models necessitates significant computational resources, limiting their accessibility for online applications. To mitigate this issue, a promising approach is model compression, which involves condensing large models into smaller, more efficient versions that can be utilized in a wide range of NLP tasks. In this study, we introduce a novel model compression technique, LATTE, which leverages a combination of fine-tuning and task-specific adaptations to transform large transformer models into smaller ones. LATTE employs a novel fine-tuning method, which involves training the model's layer 1 to adapt to the task at hand, while keeping the deeper layers frozen. To further refine the smaller model, we propose a task-specific adaptation method that involves fine-tuning specific attention heads within each transformer layer. LATTE's unique architecture allows it to maintain the performance of large models on complex tasks, such as question-answering, while significantly reducing model size. OFDM monostatic detection is commonly utilized in various radar, communication systems. However, phase distortion caused by imperfect transmission channels leads to a significant decline in detection accuracy. Existing methods either alleviate this issue or view phase distortion as an unavoidable error. This study examines a new perspective - the potential benefits of phase distortion for monostatic detection. When properly managing the phase in the frequency domain, monostatic detection can actually be enhanced. A novel low-complexity algorithm, called phase-aided monostatic detection (PAMD), has been proposed to achieve this. PAMD first estimates channel phase distortion in the frequency domain and then utilizes it to improve detection in the time domain. Simulation results demonstrate that PAMD surpasses existing methods by achieving improved detection accuracy with lower signal-to-noise ratios. Additionally, PAMD can be easily integrated into existing OFDM monostatic detection systems, offering a practical solution for phase distortion mitigation. The results of this study will pave the way for future research on how to leverage phase distortion for radar and communication systems. The process of modeling the cooling and heating effects of the interstellar medium is crucial in understanding its behavior. This study investigates whether a uniform medium model can accurately describe the cooling and heating effects, by analyzing the cooling and heating rates calculated using a more detailed inhomogeneous approach, which takes into account the varying density and temperature of the medium. Results show that for most elements, uniform and inhomogeneous models yield similar results, but when inhomogeneous effects are considered, significant differences emerge. This suggests that an earlier, simpler uniform model may have underestimated the cooling and heating rates of certain elements, particularly iron, by a substantial margin. This discrepancy highlights the need to consider the inhomogeneous approach when modeling the cooling and heating effects of the interstellar medium. An updated model incorporating these corrections is necessary to ensure accuracy for future studies. This revised model can be used to explore the interplay between the cooling and heating effects of the ISM and other physical processes, such as dust evolution and grain growth. This paper outlines the Fuel framework and presents a software development kit that facilitates the practical application of these principles in Linux kernel development. Notably, this development kit has been successfully integrated into the Linux kernel source code, and its foundational concepts have been validated through testing. Furthermore, an in-depth examination of various security features and their implementation within the Fuel structure is provided. Fuel's versatility extends beyond its current application in the Linux kernel; it can also be applied in the compilation of applications and other language platforms. The potential of real-time visual correction for enhancing video quality in fast-moving situations has garnered significant interest. This study delves into the practical applicability of visual repair in dynamic environments, with a focus on three key aspects: 1) the effectiveness of different video enhancement techniques in static and dynamic settings; 2) the minimum required resolution to accurately restore distorted frames; and 3) the capacity for visual repair systems to adapt to dynamic environments. Our research findings indicate that higher resolution is essential for visual repair systems to perform well, with a required resolution exceeding the recommended standards for high-definition television. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that these systems struggle to maintain high levels of image quality in dynamic situations, even when trained on static data. This suggests that visual repair systems may lack adaptability in dynamic environments. This study's results are expected to contribute to the development of future visual repair systems capable of handling dynamic scenes. Actuaries utilize actuarial factor models to forecast complex mortality rates. These models, which assume mortality is driven by a combination of broad factors, simplify complex mortality patterns and enable the prediction of future mortality patterns. This study examines the suitability of factor model mortality predictions for insurance applications by comparing two approaches: one that adapts to shifting factors over time and another that maintains stable factor influences. We employ a Bayesian framework to forecast mortality rates and evaluate the accuracy of these predictions through a mortality risk scoring system. Mortality predictions generated from models with time-sensitive and stable factor influences are compared across various scenarios and populations, demonstrating the effectiveness of both approaches in specific circumstances. While actuarial factor models are typically considered time-sensitive in certain instances, our research reveals that models with stable factor influences often produce more accurate predictions. These findings have important implications for the development and implementation of factor models in actuarial practice. Furthermore, our study highlights the need to consider the specific application context when deciding on the time dimension of factor models. This research contributes to the existing literature by providing a method for comparing the efficacy of factor models with time-sensitive and time-constant factor influences, which can be applied to a range of actuarial modeling scenarios. These results can be applied to a variety of insurance applications, including the pricing and reserving of long-term care products. We investigate the computational complexity of solving a class of stochastic models that determine the probability of a critical event occurring in load-balancing systems, where jobs arrive at a constant rate and are served by servers with varying lifetimes. Furthermore, the proposed framework has been shown to be compatible with existing verifiers and has the potential to be applied to more complex tasks such as semantic reasoning and natural language inference. Overall, this work represents a significant step towards establishing verifiable semantic logic for LMs and enabling more efficient and scalable AI systems. In the field of particle physics, reconstructing the characteristics of subatomic particles is a fundamental challenge, particularly within the time interval between the creation of a collision and the final data analysis stage. This issue persists due to the limited processing capacity of conventional computers and the need for rapid data processing during the data acquisition period. This research paper introduces a novel method for particle reconstruction utilizing Graph Neural Networks, specifically designed for accelerated processing on Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs). By employing a Graph Neural Network approach, the proposed system efficiently identifies neighboring particles within a cluster, calculates their proximity scores, and aggregates the necessary information to determine charged particle properties. By leveraging FPGA's reconfigurable hardware resources, the system is capable of performing a single neural network layer in a remarkably short duration, thus enabling the potential for real-time or near-real-time data analysis during the initial stages of data acquisition. This research paper introduces a pioneering approach to utilizing Graph Neural Networks for fast data processing on FPGAs and highlights the system's performance on FPGA-based devices. According to the results, the system is capable of processing multiple neural network layers in a time frame of 10 microseconds, thus enabling the potential for real-time or near-real-time data analysis. In the realm of medical imaging, specifically for analyzing coronary calcium, a significant limitation has been the non-reproducibility of results. This unreliability stems from the fact that manual measurements of coronary calcium are often time-consuming and prone to human error. This study focuses on addressing this issue by developing innovative generative models that can accurately estimate three-dimensional volumes and generate two-dimensional image slices from three-dimensional data. We evaluate the performance of these models on a large dataset comprising 1,057 coronary calcium scans and compare them to traditional methods, demonstrating their effectiveness in providing reliable and reproducible estimates of volumes and facilitating the automation of two-slice calculations. This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the reproducibility of coronary calcium assessments and contribute to more reliable patient risk stratification. We introduce SynthCity, a vast dataset comprising 400,000 synthetic point clouds of extremely high detail, with 1 million points per cloud, generated using a pipeline of deep learning models. Our goal is to assess how effectively current 3D deep learning models can be adapted and evaluated, by comparing their performance on SynthCity with its semantic segmentation labels and comparing them with leading models trained on the widely-used Semantic Segmentation Network (SfS-Net) dataset. We found that most top-performing models underperformed on SynthCity in comparison to SfS-Net, with a notable exception of Minkowski-Net, which demonstrated comparable performance on both datasets. We also discovered that models trained on synthetic data with lower resolution (100,000 points) failed to achieve satisfactory performance on SynthCity, resulting in a significant gap of around 10% IoU. To address this limitation, we made several adjustments to the training process, including using a more effective loss function, incorporating additional training data, and implementing data augmentation techniques. These modifications led to a significant improvement in performance, with the best-performing model on SynthCity achieving an IoU of 0.9423. We also conducted a series of experiments to investigate the impact of using synthetic data on real-world tasks, such as semantic segmentation, classification, and novel class detection. These studies revealed that models trained on synthetic data failed to generalize well to real-world tasks, with the largest performance gap observed in novel class detection. We believe that the current generation of deep learning models for semantic segmentation may not be adequately adapted for use with synthetic data, and we hope that our contribution will inspire further research in this area. We are releasing SynthCity, along with the corresponding code, to facilitate the development of better models for classification and novel class detection tasks. This study introduces a novel discretization method based on the max-relevance-min-variation (MRMV) criterion, aiming to optimize classification performance. The max-relevance-min-variation approach involves splitting a continuous feature into potential discrete features, selecting the optimal split, and then repeating this process for subsequent attributes. This research focuses on Statistical Compressed Sensing of image reconstruction from limited measurements of Gaussian Blend Models. A key contribution involves developing an efficient maximum likelihood estimator for GMMs under SSCS, which is highly relevant to both low-rate and high-rate compression scenarios for image sensing. Our theoretical findings demonstrate that the estimator achieves optimal reconstruction performance, as its mean-squared error is precisely equal to the measurement rate in both low and high-rate regimes. We further show that the estimator's mean-squared error is directly linked to the spectral gap of the covariance matrix of the sensing noise, which explains the phenomenon of "inversion via compression" where noisy low-rate measurements may yield better results than high-rate observations with minimal noise. Our theoretical conclusions are supported by numerical experiments conducted on real-world images. The research also explores the application of the estimator to compressive color image sensing using a single sensor. The theoretical insights and algorithms developed are highly valuable and can be extended to various sensing scenarios, even beyond Gaussian Blend Models. However, it is worth noting that the proposed estimators may still struggle with certain image reconstruction challenges, such as recovering images with prominent textures or high-frequency patterns. In response to these difficulties, this research also investigates the feasibility of leveraging deep learning techniques, such as convolutional neural networks, to enhance the performance of the estimator for specific applications like compressive color image sensing. The research concludes by discussing the potential avenues for future work in this area. This study examines the potential of machine learning algorithms in predicting financial volatility, utilizing a unique approach to financial analysis by incorporating word embeddings. This research underscores the potential of machine learning and financial word embeddings in extracting valuable information from financial markets. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the benefits of combining machine learning and financial word embeddings for informed financial analysis and effective prediction. This approach offers a valuable tool for policymakers, enabling data-driven predictions and data-informed decisions. Ultimately, by integrating mathematical modeling with real-time data analysis, it is envisioned that such frameworks can contribute significantly to mitigating future public health crises. We define a graph as geometric if its vertices coincide with the nodes of a polynomial map, with the edges represented by polynomials of degree at most 2. Geometric graphs allow for a well-studied automorphism group type, known as the W-group, which is formed by the composition of the map's automorphisms and the automorphisms of the given field. Our research focuses on establishing general upper limits for the order of the automorphism group of a given geometric graph, with the goal of characterizing the specific cases that reach these limits. Our team used the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array to observe V Hya in the 86.7 GHz CO line, capturing images of the star at different times. The observations revealed a ring structure with a diameter of approximately 170 astronomical units, located about 10 astronomical units away from the star. The ring is visible in images but not in velocity space maps, suggesting that the ring is not moving as it should be if it were a stable structure. We also observed a second ring, located on the opposite side of the star, which was not previously known. The images revealed a strong outflow of gas, which we analyzed to determine its speed and structure. The outflow of gas is moving away from the star at speeds of up to 100 kilometers per second, with a specific velocity range of 50-70 kilometers per second. We also found that the star is losing mass at a rate of 2.5 times 10^-6 times the mass of the sun per year. In a multi-armed bandit setting, we investigate a higher-level problem of dynamic learning with a unique constraint. The key novelty of our work lies in the application of a novel arm tracking technique, a new exploration function, and a new stopping rule. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications for multi-armed bandits with complex arm sequences and may inspire similar solutions for other sequential decision-making problems. However, most of these methods rely on specific patterns or features that may not be present in all images, limiting their effectiveness. In complex environments, autonomous systems often face challenges in forecasting task intentions. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Observers, which integrates a set of sample data and observation components within a Variational Autoencoder. By leveraging this method, autonomous systems can better understand task goals and predict the actions of surrounding objects. Experimental results demonstrate that our Observers model outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches in various forecasting tasks. Notably, we achieve significant gains in forecasting accuracy on our most challenging dataset. Additionally, we showcase the effectiveness of our method in predicting the intentions of autonomous driving vehicles in dense traffic scenarios. ENOS uses a dynamic method to decide whether a neural network task should be executed by the accelerator, a digital hardware accelerator, or a computer-based booster. The task of registering multiple images to a common point, time, and orientation framework is known as concurrent pose and orientation registration, where both the 3D positions and viewing angles of the images need to be determined. This problem is typically tackled using two-step approaches that first estimate the viewing angles and then the positions, but these methods can be inefficient. In this research, a new method is proposed to simultaneously determine both the viewing angles and positions of a set of images by optimizing a Resolving Viewing Graph (R-G) that models the 3D relationships between the images. To address the computational complexity of this approach, a novel method is developed to efficiently solve large-scale R-Gs. This approach is also improved by incorporating a more accurate cost function that takes into account both the local and global geometric properties of the images. This paper presents a comprehensive review of the two-step and simultaneous methods used for pose and orientation registration, and evaluates the performance of the proposed R-G method on both indoor and outdoor datasets. This result also applies to mixed digraphs. Furthermore, in the case of mixed graphs with exactly two vertices connected by a positive edge, if we consider a vertex $x$ to be part of a subgraph $G'\subset G$ that is either a cycle or a path, then the condition that the adjacency matrix of the subgraph formed by removing $x$ and $y$ and adding an edge between them has exactly two positive eigenvalues is met when and only when $G'$ is isomorphic to either a cycle or a path. This result is established using a combination of theoretical analysis and computational verification of eigenvalues for all possible cases. Computational evidence supports the possibility that the condition of having exactly two positive eigenvalues may be a complete characterization of all mixed graphs satisfying the given conditions, with the only possible exception being the ones that are isomorphic to either a cycle or a path. Self-supervised learning's growing importance stems from its ability to utilize vast amounts of unlabeled data, significantly impacting the field. Despite its benefits, there is still a need to understand the influence of various factors on self-supervised learning, particularly the disparity in training datasets. In this study, we examine how differences in dataset distribution between the training and validation sets may affect self-supervised models. Our results show that these models are more resistant to such disparities when compared to traditional supervised learning approaches. Furthermore, we found that the models' performance is heavily dependent on the initial quality of the training data, with the most impact being felt on smaller, unrepresentative datasets. While self-supervised models can adapt to certain forms of dataset disparities, they tend to underperform in cases of more substantial discrepancies. Our research also reveals that these disparities have a notable impact on model generalizability, with the largest effects being observed when the disparities are greatest. Overall, this study highlights the utility of self-supervised learning methods despite the inevitability of dataset disparities in real-world applications. Based on these findings, we propose that these methods should be considered as a means of enhancing supervised learning approaches, rather than replacing them entirely. This study introduces a probabilistic method to evaluate the performance of an aircraft that utilizes various fidelity aerodynamic data. By treating uncertain flight conditions as random variables and combining these uncertainties with high-fidelity and low-fidelity aerodynamic models, the investigation develops a cost-effective yet accurate estimation method for aircraft performance. A novel Bayesian inference approach enables the calibration of low-fidelity models using high-fidelity data and introduces a measure of model discrepancy uncertainty. This allows for the creation of accurate probabilistic estimates using low-fidelity models, which are then compared to actual aircraft performance. A proposed metric, the expected loss, reflects the potential error in performance estimation due to model inaccuracies. Case studies involving a generic aircraft and a real-life jet airliner demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in optimizing aircraft performance. By leveraging this approach, the investigation identifies the optimal balance between low-fidelity and high-fidelity aerodynamic data costs and provides insights into selecting the optimal data for real-life applications. Ultimately, the study presents a practical framework for probabilistic performance assessment of aircraft and provides recommendations for data selection. Additionally, the investigation provides a guideline for practitioners to effectively utilize this approach in practical applications. The study's code and data are publicly available for further analysis. The segmentation of brain neoplasm from MRI scans is a critical step in accurate diagnosis and treatment planning. Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have led to significant advancements in multi-modal MRI image segmentation. However, the existing methods often rely on access to all available image modalities, which is not always feasible in clinical settings. Moreover, the sensitivity of these models to missing modalities hinders their practical application. In response, we introduce a novel framework called Modality-Tier Attention Network (MTAN), which effectively handles data with missing modalities by utilizing a novel synthesis approach. This approach involves generating pseudo images from missing modalities, and then fusing the corresponding segmentation maps from different modalities through an attention mechanism. Experimental results on the BraTS 2018 dataset demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, outperforming the existing state-of-the-art methods with substantial improvements. In today's complex network landscape, Multi-Protocol Label Switching is still a dominant technology that enables fast, efficient, and flexible routing capabilities, particularly in the core internet networks. However, MPLS usage has been declining, and the increasing adoption of SDN and NFV solutions has led to its fragmentation, making it a less prominent technology in modern, software-defined networks. Consequently, skilled professionals who rely on MPLS for network monitoring, security, and troubleshooting are scarce, and the knowledge is in danger of being lost due to the shortage of experienced experts in the field.

To address this issue, we've developed TNT, a multi-layer, open-source tool that helps identify and analyze MPLS-enabled networks by actively engaging with the MPLS network infrastructure. TNT works by strategically inserting itself into a network path, allowing it to detect and analyze MPLS tunnels, monitor packet forwarding, and detect potential security threats. Additionally, TNT includes a data processing component that enables real-time data analysis and the creation of visualizations for further investigation. By providing a modern framework for TNT, we've made it easier for researchers and security professionals to use the tool in various scenarios, and the project's open-source nature is expected to help preserve knowledge related to MPLS and its evolving role in the networking landscape.
