Urban transportation network planning heavily relies on accurate bus arrival time forecasts. However, the existing literature primarily explores global models to predict bus arrival times, with only a few studies focusing on real-world applications. This paper presents a case study on developing a deep neural network-based model to forecast bus arrival times in Warsaw, Poland. The analysis utilizes historical data from one of the city's most trafficked transportation routes, with significant roadwork taking place, posing a challenge to the model's performance. The results show that the deep neural network model successfully predicts bus arrival times within a 3-minute margin of error during most periods. Notably, its effectiveness is unaffected by roadwork, indicating that the model can provide reliable forecasts even under disrupted circumstances. This study demonstrates the potential of deep neural networks in real-world bus arrival time forecasting applications. Furthermore, the findings suggest that the root cause of the larger prediction errors during roadwork is the uneven distribution of delays along the route, which is attributed to the complex spatial-temporal dynamics of the data. This insight highlights the need for further research in this area. Overall, this study confirms the adaptability of deep neural networks in real-world bus arrival time forecasting and confirms the feasibility of applying geospatial data-driven approaches to real-world applications. OTFM is an innovative modulation technique that decouples the signal processing within a transmission system, allowing for separate processing of signal structure and channel estimation. This separation enables the design of adaptable, resource-friendly receivers that can handle diverse signal architectures. In turn, these receivers can be integrated into a range of transmitters, which can be tailored to specific requirements and can even be designed to meet stringent low-latency constraints. This part of a two-part series examines various transmitter-transceiver configurations, focusing on the design possibilities that arise from the separation of signal processing functions. An accompanying part will present comprehensive performance analysis and simulation results. A surge in Chinese video analysis research has been sparked by the extensive use of video media in daily life. Nevertheless, the significant disparity between Chinese and English languages hinders the application of pre-trained language models in downstream tasks, largely due to the lack of comprehensive Chinese language resources. To bridge this gap, a substantial dataset of 48,000 Chinese video clips with 3,000 human annotators has been created for the specific purpose of enhancing video language comprehension capabilities. Our proposed model, CVL-Base, achieves impressive results in multiple tasks such as Chinese speech recognition, video text recognition, and video classification. This is accomplished through a novel pre-training method that leverages contrastive learning of multimodal features, which enables effective alignment of video and text representations despite substantial differences in their semantic spaces. Our findings demonstrate the substantial advantages of our proposed model over state-of-the-art models in various tasks, with notable improvements in fine-grained video classification, where CVL-Base outperforms the second-best model by 10.7% and outperforms the state-of-the-art model by 4.2%. Additionally, CVL-Base's pre-trained multimodal language model significantly outperforms the second-best model in video text recognition, with a relative improvement of 6.5%. The dataset and code used in this research are publicly available at the specified GitHub repository. We also plan to establish a shared task and hosting a workshop focused on CVL-Base, with the aim of fostering further research in this area. Detailed information about a person's environment is crucial for numerous applications, particularly those related to human behavior analysis. Capturing three-dimensional scenes with depth maps is a significant problem in various fields such as augmented reality, 3D scene understanding, and depth-based computer vision. Recent advancements in light field depth estimation have achieved impressive results, but there is still a gap in evaluating the accuracy of these depth maps, especially in scenes with occlusions that current techniques often struggle with. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach, the Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator (ORCE), which can effectively evaluate the accuracy of depth maps across different levels of occlusion. By analyzing the visual and geometric properties of occluded regions, ORCE provides valuable insights to help improve light field depth estimation. We demonstrate the potential of ORCE by integrating it with a state-of-the-art depth estimation network, resulting in significant performance gains. Moreover, ORCE can serve as a general framework to evaluate and improve various computer vision techniques, offering promising prospects. Our experiment involves a microcavity containing an excitonic polariton, which exhibits unique behavior when coupled with an external optical loop, resulting in a wide range of unstable laser states, including homogenous, inhomogenous, and localized pulsing. When the loop's phase is adjusted, distinct regions of instability emerge, which can be connected or disconnected by modifying the loop's phase, allowing for either homogeneous or localized pulsing. Interestingly, these regions are not only accessible through delayed feedback but also through delayed phase shifts, resulting in distinct properties, including a reduction in mode partitioning ratio, increased pulse area, and a more stable laser. This research demonstrates a simple method to control laser behavior using optical properties, which can be applied to other microcavities. Furthermore, this work has implications for controlling localized laser behavior in microcavities and may facilitate the creation of novel laser states, including localized pulsing lasers with tunable pulse properties. Ultimately, this research contributes to a deeper understanding of the behavior of excitonic polariton lasers with delayed optical feedback.
